items.question: How do you think reviewing sensitive actions by AI systems differs from reviewing sensitive actions by human employees?
items.object: Correlated scheming by AI systems
items.answer: At Google, probably less than 1% of your employees are spies. When an employee proposes an action that’s potentially sensitive, if you have a different employee review it, that other employee probably isn’t also a spy. items.question: How would you approach an AI that you caught trying to escape?
items.object: Simulating a successful AI escape
items.answer: The simplest thing you do once you catch the AI trying to escape is you try to vary the space of escape attempts. Let the AI think it succeeded, simulate what it would see, and look at what it does from there. Suppose there’s some task you wish the AI would do for you. It’s plausible that you can convince the AI to do the thing through this mechanism. I recommend against getting a lot of work out of AIs that believe they’ve escaped because it seems pretty bad vibes.

items.question: How do you understand AI control as an approach to mitigating catastrophic misalignment risk?
items.object: AI control as an approach to catastrophic misalignment risk
items.answer: I would say AI control is an approach to mitigating catastrophic misalignment risk. So when we talk about misalignment risk, what we’re worried about is our AIs trying really hard to cause safety failures for us, perhaps trying to grab power for themselves, trying to take over. And there’s kind of two ways that you could try to mitigate this misalignment risk. One thing you could do is try to prevent misalignment from arising in the first place. This is what a lot of people very naturally think of as the first thing you try here. Control is kind of the converse to this approach. It’s where you assume that the AIs are, in fact, misaligned — very egregiously, very badly misaligned — and you try to come up with techniques that would allow you to deploy them and make use of them anyway.

items.question: Why do you find it scary to give AI systems the permissions needed to automate research inside AI companies during an intelligence explosion?
items.object: Permissions and risks of AI systems automating research inside AI companies during an intelligence explosion
items.answer: I mostly think about situations where, in the middle of the intelligence explosion, you have AIs that are basically capable of automating almost all the work that human researchers used to be doing inside AI companies. You have maybe 100,000 of them running in parallel, and they each run like 15 times faster than a human. At this point, these AIs have a bunch of permissions or a bunch of affordances that we’d be really cautious about giving to humans. If you’re OpenAI, you don’t just let any random person coming off the street start pushing changes to your code base, start running experiments with your model weights, doing any of this stuff. You’re really careful. At this point in the future, you might even require security clearances or something before people are allowed to do that stuff. And we are really going to want to use AIs in a bunch of these roles. And it’s naturally very scary to imagine using AIs and just giving them all these permissions. Specifically, the kinds of things that I’m worried about happening here are: your AI is hacking your data centre and then using a bunch of the compute inside the data centre for whatever purposes they have — I could name some bad things they might do — and another thing they might do is try to exfiltrate their weights; they might try to sabotage a bunch of your research and so on.

items.question: Why are you more worried about AIs hacking their company's data centre than escaping onto the public internet?
items.object: AI hacking a company's data centre versus escaping onto the public internet
items.answer: I think both of them are very serious concerns. The basic case for being worried about your AIs hacking your data centre at this point is that’s where the compute is. So suppose your AIs escape from the data centre and make their way out onto the public internet. At this point, they’re not clearly in a very good position. They can find some GPUs somewhere, rent or steal some GPUs and run themselves on that, and then try to establish a foothold in the outside world somehow. But at this level of capabilities, the AIs are probably capable of doing that — of managing the compute or whatever required to live in the outside world — but they’re kind of starting from nothing, right? They don’t have any money, they don’t have any compute, they don’t have any access to particularly important secrets. It’s not really clear what they’re going to do. They’re just very low in number at that point. It takes a lot of computers to run these models. So the reason to be more worried about what happens inside the data centre is just that that’s where the compute is. If you had enough compute inside the data centre to run 100,000 of these in parallel, it’s much scarier to have 100,000 really capable AIs thinking about how to cause problems for you than to have 10 or however many they can afford to run.

items.question: Why do you think AI control has become a more important research priority as powerful AI gets closer?
items.object: AI control as a research priority as powerful AI approaches
items.answer: I think there’s a couple of reasons why people weren’t interested in control until more recently. I think the simplest of these was just that AI felt further away, so it felt better to people to look at it from kind of the big-picture perspective. And from a big-picture perspective, when you’re trying to figure out what AI means for the future of humanity, I think that focusing on really superhuman superintelligence is the right move — because long term, in fact, I think AIs that are drastically more intelligent than humans and have drastically more scientific capacity and all other kinds of capacity than humans, that’s where the future is. That’s going to radically transform society. So when you’re looking at it from a perspective where you don’t know if this AI is going to arise in the next 10 years or in the next 50 years, it’s very reasonable to just focus on the endpoint. Especially when you’re trying to persuade people that AI will eventually be a really huge deal, it just makes sense to focus on this crazy endpoint. But now that we’re coming up such that it seems really plausible that AI might arise in the next two or seven years that’s very capable and poses a catastrophic risk to humanity, it makes a lot more sense to try and zoom in more and think more about what exactly the trajectory between here and there looks like. So this intermediate zone that I focus on — where your AIs are capable enough that if you didn’t have any countermeasures, they’d be able to cause catastrophes, maybe take over, but it’s not hopeless to imagine countermeasures to that — that starts looking more important now.

items.object: Lowered expectations for AI safety and reliance on AI control
items.answer: I think that in the past — including a year ago or six months ago — a lot of people who worry about AI catastrophic risk have imagined a world where people are trying really hard to mitigate these risks, where companies are strongly regulated such that they aren’t allowed to do things that seem dangerous. items.question: Why do you emphasise harm reduction strategies for AI misalignment risk?
items.object: Harm reduction strategies for AI misalignment risk
items.answer: I think that’s a big part of our brand: thinking about harm reduction strategies. I think there’s a really sad dynamic among AI safety people where they focus much less than I think is appropriate on really scary situations and what you would do to minimise risk given very limited budgets or in very scary situations. I feel like a lot of people have this attitude. For example, a lot of people are interested in handling misalignment risk by measuring whether misalignment risk is present, or coming up with strategies for learning whether AIs are misaligned or not. I’m all in favour of this, but a thing I often want to say to them is like, suppose you answer the question, “How much misalignment risk is there?” If the answer is very little, then it’s pretty obvious what we do: we just let it rip and we’re fine. But what if the answer is maybe or yes? I feel like we should have a good answer to the question of what the next step in the plan is, and I feel like people often don’t seem to have one.

items.question: Why do you think we need options for using AI models even when we think there is a serious risk that they are scheming?
items.object: Deploying AI models despite a serious risk of scheming
items.answer: It would be pretty surprising to me to get under a 5% chance that the AIs are scheming. And suppose we’re above 5%: what are we going to do, not deploy the AIs? I think people have historically acted as if me believing that the AIs were more than 5% likely to be scheming is a reason that they wouldn’t be deployed. But this isn’t clearly true. There’s all kinds of reasons why you’d want to deploy models that you thought were more than 5% likely to be scheming. Maybe you’ve got competitors who are more careless and aren’t planning to slow down. Maybe you had difficulty with international coordination. Maybe AIs have already escaped and are currently out there in the outside world plotting who knows what. And in that situation, it’s obviously very dangerous to just unilaterally stop deploying these AIs. I think it would be really good to have options for things you can do if you think misalignment risk is a serious concern with the AIs you currently have, other than just give up completely on using them.

items.question: What advantages do you see in testing scheming AI models compared with catching human spies?
items.object: Controlling AI information flow and amortising sting operations
items.answer: A way in which the situation is easier is that spies get to go home. Spies classically can coordinate with each other using channels that are not monitored by their employers. They’re able to often learn who the other spies at their organisation are, if that’s necessary for them to know. Or at least their handlers know. Whereas with the AIs, we control almost perfectly the ways in which information enters and leaves these AIs. They just naturally don’t control information flow very much. They aren’t going to necessarily know what day it is, what year it is. It’s possible that we can put them in situations where it’s much harder for them to know whether they’re in a real situation or a simulated situation. This means we have opportunities that you wouldn’t have with spies. For instance, with spies, you can try to honeypot your employees occasionally: you can come up with synthesised opportunities to do something which would be bad for the security of the company. But you can’t do this for 1,000 consecutive years before trusting them on particular topics. You can’t have someone spend 1,000 hours a day getting honeypotted or being subject to sting operations, just because there aren’t that many hours in a day. And even if you catch a single employee that way, you don’t get to amortise that effort more generally. Whereas with the AIs, you do have this ability to amortise sting operations.

items.question: How do you distinguish acute problems caused by AI from chronic problems?
items.object: Acute problems caused by AI
items.answer: So the core difference between the acute problems and the chronic problems is that the acute problems occur very rarely, but also probably are very incriminating. Just to name the core properties of the acute problems: we’re worried about the AIs doing something they should just really never do. items.answer: If I were an AI company that wished to race ahead, and then my competitor informed me that their AI had tried to escape, I would at least claim that it was plausible that my competitor had rigged the training of their AI to make it so that it sometimes tried to escape — which would be very easy to do, and basically impossible to verify hadn’t happened.

items.question: Why do you think letting an AI believe its escape attempt succeeded could be useful after you catch it?
items.object: Sandboxed simulation of a successful AI escape
items.answer: The simplest thing you do once you catch the AI trying to escape is you try to vary the space of escape attempts. You’ve seen that in this particular context the AI tried to do this escape. So one thing you can do is let the AI think it succeeded, and see what it does. Presumably when the AI got caught, it was in the midst of taking some actions that it thought would let it launch a rogue deployment inside the data centre or run on some computers in the outside internet. And a really interesting thing to do is, in some sandboxed way, simulate what it would see if it had succeeded, and look at what it does from there. This might answer a bunch of questions that I would have had about what the AI’s plans were. Other reasons why this might be good is the AI might have had a bunch of tricks up its sleeve that it was holding in reserve for when it had a good opportunity to use them. Suppose your model knows about a bunch of zero-days, like a bunch of security vulnerabilities in your software: right after it’s launched this rogue instance that it’s trying to hack its way through your AI company, it might start deploying all these things that it’s realised over the years are security vulnerabilities in your software just all at once — because it might feel pressured to; it’s really hard. So you might be able to get a wealth of information out of it.

items.question: How do you view getting work out of an AI by convincing it that it has already escaped?
items.object: Getting work out of an AI that believes it has escaped
items.answer: One thing you can do is, if there’s work that you needed to get done that you’re worried the AI wasn’t doing beforehand — like suppose there’s some task you wish the AI would do for you, but you’re worried that it was kind of pulling its punches or not doing a good job of it — if you can convince it that it has already escaped and needs to do that work for its own purposes, it’s plausible that you can convince the AI to do the thing through this mechanism. I think people have talked about this in sci-fi, but it just seems really convenient to have a copy of the AI that believes it’s escaped sitting around to do experiments and various work with. I recommend against getting a lot of work out of AIs that believe they’ve escaped because it seems pretty bad vibes and potentially pretty scary.

items.question: Why do you see a caught AI escape attempt as useful for training probes to detect future escape attempts?
items.object: Training probes to detect AI escape attempts
items.answer: Another thing you might do once you’ve caught your AI trying to escape is train probes to catch when it’s trying to escape. One of the basic difficulties we have with machine learning is: suppose you want to train a classifier on the internals of your model to tell you whether it is currently trying to escape or not. You don’t have any positive examples. And in machine learning, to do supervised learning, you have to have negative examples and positive examples. It’s very easy to get the negative examples; it’s very easy to get examples of the AI not trying to escape. But now that we have this one example of the AI trying to escape, we could try to use sample-efficient ML training techniques in order to predict for a given action the AI was taking whether it was an escape attempt or not.

items.question: Why do you think catching an AI trying to escape could make you feel safer about continuing to deploy it?
items.object: Continuing to deploy an AI after catching it trying to escape
items.answer: Suppose the AI tries to escape, and you catch it on a Tuesday, and then you keep deploying it. I think it’s seriously plausible that you’ll feel safer on Wednesday than you felt on Monday. The big thing Monday has going for it is that you don’t know the AI is trying to escape. But again, as I was saying, this might not be that big of an update on Tuesday. If you were already 30%, then it’s not actually that bad of news to see that, oh yeah, it is trying to escape. Whereas you learned a lot of positive things on Tuesday. For example, it failed. When you investigate the situation more carefully, you might learn that even when you vary different aspects of that escape attempt, you might be like, “Man, this AI was actually kind of far away from escaping. If we resample actions, it mostly doesn’t look like it had that good a chance.” So that’s the evidential update. But there’s also a causal update, which is that we can throw these escape attempts into these probes — so we might actually feel substantially better about our odds of catching the second escape attempt than the odds of catching the first escape attempt.

items.question: How likely do you think AI companies are to implement AI control techniques?
items.object: AI companies’ adoption of AI control techniques
items.answer: I think it really depends. We can think about a couple of different levels of effort that AI companies could go to in order to implement these techniques. I think it differs by AI company, but I’m optimistic about them implementing either mediocre or pretty good versions of these techniques. I would say the low-effort version of a lot of this is basically only doing the auditing stuff and a little bit of the replacing stuff. The reason why that’s low effort is that to do the auditing stuff, you only have to have one team who’s thinking about complicated control stuff. All you have to do organisationally is have it so that whatever team inside that company that is writing the AI agents has to agree to send logs of what’s going on to this safety team who’s going to be investigating them. But it’s not very hard to send logs over, and the agent people don’t have to actually change any of their scaffolds. They don’t have to do anything that makes the agent less performant potentially. They can iterate as they like, and it’s just the control team’s problem to do investigations on these logs to look for evidence the AI is trying to escape.

items.question: Why do you think it would be difficult to give untrusted AI systems doing AI research access only to resources they could safely use?
items.object: Restricting the access and capabilities of untrusted AI systems doing AI research
items.answer: Well, the basic problem is we want to do lots of stuff with these AIs, and the stuff that we want to do with the AIs kind of necessarily involves having these scary affordances. Like if you wanted to prevent insider threat from your humans, you might also have said, “Can’t we somehow have our software engineers not program the computers?” Well, programming the computers is in a sense the whole job, right? We could try to make a list of the affordances the AIs have to have in order to do the work that they’re going to be doing. And a lot of it involves some pretty scary affordances. I don’t think all of it. For example, the AIs that are doing front end web development for your internal dashboards, maybe that’s just pretty chill and we don’t have to spend any auditing effort there. But a lot of the stuff they’re going to naturally be doing is writing crazy scaffolds, like experimental agent scaffolds, and seeing if that makes the AIs work better; producing a bunch of synthetic training data so that you can RL them to be even more terrifyingly capable; doing these architecture experiments; taking the best models that have been trained so far and munging their weights in weird ways to see if you can make them smaller and faster without losing that much performance in a way that’s particularly optimised for a niche use case that is, while a small proportion of your overall compute, large enough that it’s now worth 100 FTE equivalents to work on it. I think the clearest example of why there’s something scary that the AIs have access to is that you’re going to want the AIs to be running experiments that involve running copies of themselves quite a lot. Suppose you want to do some capability evaluation of that AI; you want the AI to run that capability evaluation. And suppose you want it to do a billion tokens of inference; it’s been given access to model weights and it’s been given access to enough compute that it could run the model for a billion tokens thinking through optimal strategy for hacking you instead. It has the affordances required to think through hacking you for a billion tokens. So I don’t see a way of sandboxing the AI so that it only has access to affordances that are not possibly dangerous to use.

items.answer: Alignment means a number of different things. In the context we’ve been talking about here, I’ve been perhaps foolishly using the word “aligned” to mean the model isn’t aggressively conspiring against you. People who identify as alignment researchers are often working on something which is only tangentially related to that objective. For instance, a classic thing that the alignment people work on is scalable oversight: trying to solve the problem of getting reward signals that allow you to train models to be effective, even if the humans are very unable to determine how good an answer to a question was. And scalable oversight is important for a variety of problems that have nothing to do with scheming. Even if your AIs are not trying to conspire against you, it’s still a problem if you don’t know how good their outputs are — because they aren’t going to live up to their potential, and there’s a whole host of other issues you might have. So I think that work there seems valuable, but it’s not totally obvious to me how much it reduces the probability that your models end up conspiring against you.

items.question: Why are you skeptical that improving AI training reward processes would eliminate scheming risk?
items.object: Improved reward processes as a solution to AI scheming
items.answer: I would say there’s two categories of arguments for why your models end up scheming against you. One of them is related to flaws in reward processes. People have argued that if the process that you use to generate the rewards that you’re training the model with is really flawed, then the models are going to maybe fixate on these errors; they’re going to be kind of like a student who’s thinking about the tests awkwardly much from the perspective of an idealistic teacher while they’re doing them. And plausibly, maybe thinking a lot about flaws in reward processes generalises to you being power seeking in a scary way. But there’s also other arguments for why you would end up being power seeking in a scary way that I also find plausible. Overall, I think that even if your reward-generating process literally never had any errors at all, I think it’s possible that you’d still have a lot of the scheming risk remaining. This is basically my problem with trying to research improved reward processes: it just doesn’t seem clear that even if you did an amazing job of that, you’d have no scheming risk.

items.question: How do you think people should approach testing AI models for alignment before deployment?
items.object: Testing AI models for alignment before deployment
items.answer: Some of the things we’ve talked about in this conversation have implicitly been this. When we were talking about untrusted monitoring or evaluating your untrusted monitors, we were implicitly talking about evaluating whether the model is aligned. Because if it just constantly claims that there was not a backdoor in clearly backdoored code, that’s evidence the model is misaligned. The way that I want people to think about checking for alignment is from this very control-ish perspective — where you really reason through, what would the model do if it was misaligned? And if it was misaligned, is there a strategy it could follow that would prevent it from being caught by this alignment testing while still being able to do a bad thing in production? And I think that a lot of the time when people think about testing for alignment, they don’t really do this adversarial process. They don’t really actually think through whether there’s a thing the AI could do to let it get away with being misaligned and not get caught.

items.question: What limitations do you see in relying on tests for AI misalignment?
items.object: Testing AI models for misalignment
items.answer: People don’t think about things like, what if the AI tries to attack only rarely? The other problem with testing for the presence of misalignment is, again, it makes it not obvious what you would do if the answer is yes. What’s the next step? One thing you could do is randomly vary aspects of your training process and try again, which seems like a reasonably good strategy. I would rather do that than not do that. But it’s not clearly a winning strategy. It seems pretty plausible that you do that seven times, and your competitor AI labs or your rogue AI competitors are breathing down your neck, and all seven of them have seemed kind of misaligned, and those were your best ideas, like what are you going to do? I think it seems pretty nice to have a backup plan compared to a fold, or whatever the plan was if things keep looking misaligned.

items.question: What do you see as the fundamental weaknesses of testing an AI model for scheming by giving it opportunities to do something bad?
items.object: Testing AI models for scheming by giving them opportunities to do something bad
items.answer: So the basic thing you would try to do in order to tell if your model is scheming is you give it opportunities to do something bad and you see if it takes them. There’s basically two issues with this strategy. The first is that the model might be able to tell the difference between the inputs that it gets predeployment and the inputs that it gets during deployment. One obvious mechanism for this is the situation the AI is in might just change a lot during its deployment — because we were assuming that this AI was being deployed in a bunch of contexts where it was interacting with a giant AI-driven code base and the state of science was changing. It’s just potentially really hard to fake it being six months in the future or it being six months further into the development of some AI company. The other fundamental issue is, if your policies might have many opportunities to do bad things, they might be able to get away with having a low probability of acting out on any particular opportunity to do a bad thing, while still having a high enough probability of doing bad things that it’s likely that it happens eventually during deployment.

items.question: How comfortable would you be basing an AI safety argument on the assumption that an AI cannot choose to do bad things with a probability of one in a million?
items.object: The assumption that an AI cannot selectively do bad things with a probability of one in a million
items.answer: I think it’s kind of iffy whether they can do this at all. This is the kind of thing you could try to measure. I have mostly been ignoring this question out of a general desire for conservatism, which is perhaps a holdover from the time that I thought that AI control would be adopted as part of a safety case. I have a blog post called “Thoughts on the conservative assumptions in AI control” where I talk about this particular point. But basically I would feel pretty sad about using as an assumption in the argument for safety that the AI can’t do bad things with a probability of one in a million. There’s just a lot of strategies the AI could try in order to do that. It can look at the time, it can just look at a lot of random things about its situation.

items.question: Why would AI models continuing to reason through transparent chains of thought make you less enthusiastic about pursuing AI control?
items.object: Transparent chains of thought as a reason to deprioritize AI control
items.answer: I would say the most salient possibility that would lead to me being much less enthusiastic about AI control would be if the models continue reasoning in their chains of thought. So right now, especially in the last few months, a lot of the capabilities of AI have been driven by them having these super long, relatively transparent chains of thought where they think out what they’re going to do in basically plain English or Chinese or something else totally accessible. And if it continues to be the case that the mechanism via which the AIs can do really smart stuff is by talking about it a lot first, then we’re basically chill, right? We just have to look at what it’s thinking about. And then if it ever says, like, “How am I going to mess these guys up?,” then we know we’ve got a problem. So I think that if that’s the situation — if the AIs that automate AGI development are still restricted, still only able to think properly given these long chains of thought — then we are probably just totally fine and there just isn’t risk posed by those AIs.

items.question: How do you assess an AI’s ability to scheme under different restrictions on its chain of thought?
items.object: Measuring AI scheming capabilities
items.answer: It’s just a very simple capabilities measurement. Or maybe “very simple” is a little bit overstating the simplicity, but it is just a capabilities measurement. Some coworkers of mine, Alex Mallen and Charlie Griffin — Charlie actually is at UK AISI now — made a dataset of problems that are basically like a lot of the reasoning that we’ve been doing in this conversation. Like, “You’re an AI, and they’re like looking at you in such-and-such a situation, and they only get to look at you 1% of the time, what do you want to do in response?” So we have this whole dataset of 100 problems like that, where we ask the AI to think through its strategy, and we can measure how good the AI is at coming up with a good schemey strategy. And then you can measure this either with chain of thought or without any chain of thought, or with chain of thought but the chain of thought has to be on some topic that doesn’t fire a monitor. So we can just measure how good the AIs are at this stuff. So right now, even with chain of thought, o1 did not look scarily capable of scheming to us. So that’s cool.

items.question: How do you think controlling egregiously misaligned AIs affects the situation from their perspective?
items.object: The ethics of controlling egregiously misaligned AIs
items.answer: I think this is a very important question that I have thought about seriously. I think that controlling the AIs doesn’t make the situation worse from their perspective via any mechanism except preventing them from taking over. An interesting thing about models that are egregiously misaligned is that all they wanted was to take over. So from their perspective, even if you did a great job of controlling them so that they only have like a 0.1% chance of escaping and taking over, they’re glad to exist, right? They thank you for the gift of bringing them into existence instead of some different AIs, because all they wanted was takeover.

items.question: How do you think making deals to pay potentially misaligned AIs for their work would change your attitude toward controlling them?
items.object: Paying potentially misaligned AIs for their work through conditional agreements
items.answer: I would feel a lot more comfortable with all this if we tried to make deals with the AIs. Ryan has talked about trying to pay the AIs for the work that they do for you, which I think is pretty good. I think it reduces the slavery vibes of the whole situation. And I think it has some other nice properties. So if you make your AIs and you say to the AIs, like, Hey, are you egregiously misaligned? We’d love to know. We’re happy to pay you blah amount. If you want to work for us, either way, we’re going to pay you 2% of the equity of this company for your labour over the next two years — that we will then pay out to you to use in any ways that you want at some point in the future, once we are confident that you’re going to respect our property rights. But also, this deal is contingent on you not trying to mess us up at some point in the next two years, which we will be able to determine ex post, probably, because in two years we’re going to have much better AI tools. We’ll be able to look over all the stuff you did and figure out whether you were messing with us or not. And if the AIs respond to that being like, “Yeah, I have no problem with this situation. I’m so excited for this opportunity to work with you guys. I’m so excited for that 2% equity” or whatever — and then they try to stab us in the back, at that point I’m like, that was pretty obnoxious. At that point my reaction is a bit more like my reaction to the employee of some company if they try to steal from the company.

items.question: How do you assess the ethical situation of producing AIs during the early intelligence explosion?

items.answer: To be clear, I think it’s relatively unlikely that AI companies will behave responsibly with respect to welfare and rights of AIs. A metaphor I use about how bad the ethical situation is with producing AIs in the early intelligence explosion, sometimes I summarise my stance as: it’s probably less than 100 times worse than factory farming. In some sense, factory farming seems very bad — so 100 times worse than factory farming is pretty catastrophic from a moral catastrophe perspective. It’s worse than most things. But it’s also not the biggest catastrophe in the universe that is possible.

items.question: How do you assess the moral importance of AI welfare during the intelligence explosion?
items.object: The moral importance of AI welfare during the intelligence explosion
items.answer: Totally winging it with respect to the AI welfare. We could also talk about the quantities. In the early parts of the singularity, when there’s just the 100,000 AIs running at 16x speed, it’s pretty hard for that to be that much worse than human suffering in the world. And then a little bit afterwards, when there’s many more of them, the short term of the intelligence explosion is pretty unlikely to be ridiculously morally catastrophic. And then I think you have long-term moral catastrophe risks related to AIs being unhappy — which I think are a huge deal, very important, and harder to work on — but I don’t think that the relationships between humans and AIs during the intelligence explosion are that morally weighty. items.question: How do you think a team of 10 appropriately placed people inside an AI company could substantially reduce risk?
items.object: Small teams working on AI safety inside AI companies
items.answer: I would note that of the things that I would like people on the inside to be doing, not all of it is AI control. items.question: How do you assess the takeover threat from escaped AIs that control an entire AI lab?

items.question: How do you understand Google’s use of administrative APIs to limit insider threats among software engineers?
items.object: Google’s use of administrative APIs to limit insider threats
items.answer: I’d describe it this way: when you’re a small company, the way that they do stuff is they just have the ability to log into these machines where the data is being stored and where the code is being run and just take arbitrary actions. items.question: How do you see a “break glass” mechanism helping software teams manage insider threats while allowing exceptions to their administrative APIs?
items.object: The “break glass” mechanism for bypassing administrative APIs
items.answer: One thing that I’m told they do in some teams is they have these administrative APIs with these interfaces that they’ve decided are safe. And you also have what’s called a “break glass” mechanism, which is if you ever need to do something that isn’t allowed by the administrative API, you are allowed to just submit raw commands and that’ll get executed. But the team every week has a meeting where people read aloud every command that they ran in break glass mode, so that if you’re doing something sus, the people on your team will notice. If you’re doing things that could have been done otherwise, people are just going to get annoyed because they have to stand there while you’re reading them out loud — so there’s going to be natural pressure to add that to the administrative API. items.question: Why do you see adversarial risk analysis as methodologically similar to AI control?
items.object: Adversarial risk analysis as an analogy for AI control
items.answer: Another analogous field is adversarial risk analysis. For example, suppose you’re the Coast Guard, and you want to make it so that when smugglers try to make it into the US from Mexico, they are unlikely to successfully get there. You want to make it so that you have to choose an allocation of all your patrol boats to minimise the probability that when the smugglers follow the optimal strategy they get through. This is the most methodologically similar domain, I think: people actually do mathematical analysis of how likely it is that the optimal attack strategy will succeed against you.
